summary:
This is a design study. I ran no scoring lives and changed no repo files. My task assigned me no seed blocks, so the one measurement I made is a diagnostic only: 256 lives, 24 CPU-s, 1 thread, seeds 49,000,000-49,000,031 (outside the study's 43M range). It was not used to compare bodies. Script and output: /home/jgon/project/ml/cell-dev/outputs/openhr/opendesign/d0_speed.py and d0_speed.json.

What it found (SPECK, d0 0.5):
- The reflex@hollow3 dot moves about 0.28-0.30 units per time unit along its path.
- Its captures per life are 21.4 / 17.6 / 10.8 / 6.2 at target speeds 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.4.
- A life has about 41 target placements: about 21 captures plus 20 timer re-placements, because the timer runs regardless of captures.
These numbers set the proposed speed limits for prey. They also show that prey fitness can be measured per placement at no extra cost: the generation's top 64 bodies produce about 18,000 placement outcomes per generation.

What I read:
- kernel.c's CATCH accountant: place, world_turn, world_to, catch_click, catch_candidate, catch_start, run_one.
- LIFE_ABI 4.7 and 9.7.
- evaluate.py: LifeDraw already gives every genome the same world in each life slot, so per-slot prey keys need no kernel change.
- build.run; the ROADMAP; TASK_VARIATION_PLAN sections 1-6; POST_PILOT_CALLS, including why the c_miss ramp was dropped.
- The prior scratch results (capabilities, headroom, nichemap/table_compact.md).
- make_xkernel.py, and engineering/kernel_x.c with xref.py. kernel_x already has per-blob brightness, mid-life re-heading and telegraph epochs; it is 116 diff lines plus a 236-line Python mirror, and it is what my effort estimates are scaled from.
- The parallel agents' measuring-stick tools: openhr/harness (the information-test controller) and openhr/gradient/gdfe.py (the mutant test).

Main conclusion. Every hand-built gate made our design skill the ceiling for one reason: it asked whether a body we built could win at a fixed difficulty. It never let a population meet a gentle version of a hard world and follow it as it hardened. Two options fix that without our having to build the solution:
- **Coevolving prey.** A world that responds to the population through an opponent with its own fitness.
- **A gated world archive.** The user's three measuring sticks become the rule for which worlds enter.

Both make the world depend on how the population is doing. That is the one property the dropped c_miss ramp shared with them. The other parts of the ramp are absent here: nobody chooses a direction, thresholds or a lesson, and no price ever moves. The user needs to decide that explicitly.

Caveats:
- No prey kernel has been built.
- The information and gradient tests against prey have not been run. I list them as gates before launch.
- Engineering estimates come from reading the code and from the size of those earlier prototypes.
- CPU estimates use the plan's 0.065-0.16 s per life and my diagnostic.
- The literature evidence comes from the research agent, and some primary sources were unverified. The strongest coevolution result (Zaman 2014, 17/50 vs 0/50) is in Avida. In neural predator-prey work (Nolfi & Floreano) the populations often cycled, so expectations should be modest.

options.name: Coevolving prey: evasive targets with their own genome, reduced virulence, hall of fame
options.what_changes:
WORLD and KERNEL (Stage 1 only):
- The Blob struct (kernel.c, about line 229) gains prey state: genome row, brightness, speed mode, stamina, one slow internal variable, and the next look time and index.
- world_to (about line 1359) gets a third world-event kind, 'look', ordered after timer and turn.
- A new world_look(), modelled on world_turn (about line 1346), reads dot_at() the way place() already does. A ~40-weight network with softsign activation (so no new libm call) sets heading, speed and brightness.
- catch_candidate (about line 1598) multiplies lam_s*halo by the prey's brightness, as kernel_x's amp_eff already does. lambda_max is unchanged because brightness <= 1.
- place() (about line 1326) picks the prey row by hash(seed, S_PREY, q) and resets stamina.
- Optional startle: a miss near the prey triggers a deferred look, done like defer_place.
- New life_run input: a prey table [n_prey x K]. New output: per-prey placements, captures, exposure, dark time and sprint time.
- About 8 world keys for the limits and the mixture (ABI 4).
- reference.py mirror (an xref.py-style _Accountant subclass first), a lifesim.js port, and a null-prey test: a table that reproduces run-and-tumble must give ABI-3 lives bit for bit.

OUTER LOOP:
- A prey population of 16, (mu+lambda) with 4 replaced per generation, and reduced-virulence fitness (lambda 0.75).
- Prey fitness comes from the shortlist's placement outcomes on the generation's own lives: 64 bodies x 7 lives x ~40 placements, about 560 placements per current prey per generation.
- A hall-of-fame snapshot every 10 generations. Yardsticks every 25 generations against fixed held-out prey and the base world.
- Body selection is unchanged: plain mean F, prices fixed (R_cap 500, c_miss 10, c_live 0.02).

STAGE 0:
- Per-slot world vectors in LifeDraw, plus a scratch hook that keeps per-life captures (columns() has them; LifeEval keeps only means).
- 7 slots per generation, a prey population of 14, each prey scored on 64 shortlisted bodies.
- Score: x = 1 - (shortlist captures on that prey) / (its captures on the base slots of the same generation).
- Reuses engineering/fam_eval.py and evolve_x.py.
options.locality:
Prey are world physics computed by the accountant, like today's target. The prey sensing the dot is the world reading itself: place() and catch_click() already read dot_at.

Cells still receive only receptor pings at their own screen point, d_min after the candidate. No cell reads the prey genome, the prey's state, the mixture or the population.

Each prey change belongs to one object, with its own random phase (plan 2.5's rule). Brightness scales that prey's halo, not lam_bg, so nothing acts as a body-wide broadcast.

Prey draws and prey randomness are keyed by (life seed, placement index, look index). So every body in a generation meets the same prey sequence (common random numbers), and lives replay exactly under both schedulers.
options.user_decision:
1. THE CORE QUESTION: may the world respond to the population?
- Like the dropped c_miss ramp, prey make the world depend on how well bodies are doing.
- Unlike it, nobody picks the direction, the steps, the thresholds or the lesson, and no price ever moves. Prey change only because their own fitness pays them to escape.
- You listed co-evolving opponents as a later direction. This asks whether 'later' is now.

2. THE PREY'S PHYSICAL LIMITS. Each is needed because without it prey become trivially uncatchable and selection loses its gradient:
- cruise speed <= 0.2 and sprint <= 0.3, both paid from stamina. Measured: the reflex's dot moves about 0.29 per time unit, and its captures halve between target speeds 0.1 and 0.3.
- noticing radius <= 3, measured from the dot's centre. The centre rather than the body's edge, so prey add no new size penalty.
- at most one look per time unit;
- a dimming floor: 0.25, or 0, which lets prey vanish (that is the blink world);
- startle at a nearby miss: yes or no;
- a decoy that mimics the target, only at a price-neutral value (clicking it costs exactly c_miss).

3. PREY FITNESS: reduced virulence with lambda 0.75 (recommended), or a minimal criterion: a prey counts only if the generation's best body still catches it at some minimum rate.

4. THE MIXTURE: 25 / 50 / 25 (base / current / hall of fame).

5. ABI 4 for the repo version: a new kernel input and output, mirrored in reference.py and lifesim.js.
options.engineering_pd: Stage 0 (scratch, existing keys): 2-3 pd, plus 1 pd for the blink/dark keys via a rebuilt xkernel (make_xkernel's patches predate the LIFE_FAST block). Stage 1 scratch (kernel plus an xref-style Python mirror, checked bit for bit): 3-4 pd. Repo grade (kernel.c, reference.py, lifesim.js, ABI 4 doc, null-prey and equivalence tests): 8-11 pd. Scaled from kernel_x, which already has per-blob brightness and mid-life re-heading in 116 diff lines plus a 236-line Python mirror.
options.cpu:
About 1.05-1.20x today's generation (about 110-130 CPU-s against about 107).
- Prey selection reuses the generation's own lives.
- Looks add about 1,000 cheap world events per life against 10^5-10^6 kernel events, under 2%.
- Yardsticks (4 bodies x 256 lives every 25 generations) add about 4%.
- An information-test check of current prey every 50 generations adds about 1% if the controller is only re-scored, or 5-15% if it is re-tuned each time.
- Hidden cost: as prey get harder, captures per life fall, so each life carries less selection information. Keeping today's precision late in a run may need 1.3-2x lives.
risks: Disengagement. Evasion is easier than pursuit (Cliff & Miller), and c_miss 10 makes blind clicks expensive, so bodies may shrink and stop clicking. Mitigations: reduced virulence, 25% base targets, physical limits. Monitors: shortlist captures on current prey relative to base targets, and the spread of F across the population.
Cycling between prey tricks and counter-tricks (Nolfi & Floreano saw limit cycles). Mitigations: a 25% hall of fame and master-tournament plots.

Prey exploit world physics: drifting outside the placement ring, sitting in the hollow body's blind interior (legitimate), dimming to the floor. Stamina and limits bound these; any real loophole is a world bug to fix and rerun (Sims's warning).
Prey find tricks that no local tissue can answer. The periodic information test flags it: if the controller no longer beats the best reflex on current prey, prey have gone past the edge.
'Be smaller' when prey are hard. Keep the plan's guards: end size, the F-size correlation, hollow2 vs hollow3.
Fewer captures per life means noisier ranking; POOL already has only about 13 captures per life.
Over-specialisation: bests that beat only their own run's prey. Held-out prey are required.
The prey genome space is bounded by design (POET's plateau). The policy is a small network rather than a menu of named tricks, but its actions and limits are still our choices.
Exactness: the policy must use no new transcendental function (softsign, not tanh), or kernel, reference and JS may diverge bit-wise.
The evidence is mixed: Avida's strong result is for logic functions, while neural predator-prey studies often cycled or produced champions that simple specialists could beat.
options.beyond_hand_evidence:
Pre-registered, on 1,024 fresh lives from blocks assigned for this purpose:
- The final best of arm C beats every hand body by more than 3 SE: reflex@hollow3 frozen and re-tuned, program and grown routers frozen and re-tuned, regen7, and the best hand body re-tuned against the final prey archive on separate tuning lives. This must hold on:
  (a) its run's final prey mixture;
  (b) held-out prey: other seeds' final prey, scripted prey (flee, swerve, hide, fast-straight, mimic) and 64 random prey genomes within the limits;
  (c) the base world, where it must lose no more than 1 F against arm B's best.
- A lesion removes at least 50% of the lead: lateral_off; hidden_off costing more than 0.5 F at z > 3 (the first job for the hidden planes); or a genes_blind fork after a prey switch (within-life adaptation).
- The information controller beats the best reflex against the same prey, and the evolved body closes at least half of that gap.
- Zaman's feedback test: C > R (prey replayed without feedback) and C > D (the same prey space at random) on (a) and (b), across 12 seeds.
- A master tournament (bodies from generation g against prey from generation g') shows net progress, not cycling.
- The probe battery shows a response the reflex lacks, named only afterwards: for example, the body keeps moving after the halo vanishes, or leads a moving spot.

options.name: Minimal-criterion world archive (PLR/ACCEL replay, admitted by the three measuring sticks)
options.plain_explanation:
Keep a small archive of up to 8 worlds besides the base world. A new world is a small random mutation of an archived world's task keys. Prices never mutate, and d0 stays fixed because it is cell physics. The mutable keys include the scratch keys the old plan excluded: blink duty, dark luminance, motor-flip timing, decoy epochs, fast straight targets.

A candidate world is admitted while three measurements agree:
1. The information-test controller beats the best reflex there, so the information is in the sense stream and the world pays for using it.
2. Some random mutants of current bests improve there without shrinking or clicking less, so there is a gradient. This is a rank weight, not a veto, because Lenski found harmful stepping stones.
3. The best evolved body still trails the controller, so the world is not yet solved. The gap is capped, so worlds that seem to need instant whole-body pooling are not chased.

Each generation, some life slots replay archived worlds, chosen by rank of that gap and of learnability; 25% stay base. When a world's gap closes it retires and counts as solved (an ANNECS-like count). There is one population, not POET's population per world.
options.what_changes:
WORLD and KERNEL:
- None for repo keys.
- Within-life keys come from a rebuilt scratch xkernel, or from kernel_x: telegraph epochs, flicker, payoff swap and motor sign, already checked bit for bit against xref.py.
- The repo-grade version is the plan's gated epoch bundle.

OUTER LOOP:
- The archive, plus ACCEL-style mutation of 1-2 keys of high-gap worlds.
- Replay sampling inside LifeDraw, as per-slot worlds hash-keyed like the plan's family draw, so common random numbers and resume hold.
- An admission pipeline on top of openhr/harness (controllers C0-C3, best_reflex, paired) and openhr/gradient/gdfe.py (mutant screen, re-score, replicate).
- PATA-EC novelty on a fixed archive of bodies (reflex hollow2 and hollow3, re-tuned reflex, program and grown routers, regen7, s5, s7, current bests).
- An ANNECS log and fixed held-out yardsticks.
options.locality: Worlds are per-life key vectors, fixed for each life. In-life rules are untouched. Within-life switches follow plan 2.5: a telegraph process with a stationary start, cues that belong to objects, and no switching of prices. The central controller and the mutant panels are measurement only, run on their own seed blocks, and never become part of an organism.
options.engineering_pd: Scratch: 5-7 pd (archive and replay 2-3, admission pipeline on the existing harness and gdfe 2-3, novelty and logs 1). Repo grade: 10-13 pd, including the epoch bundle (3.5-4 pd) and its JS port (1-1.5 pd).
options.cpu:
Body lives cost the same (1.0x). Each candidate screen costs about 0.3-0.5 CPU-h: reflex re-tune about 0.1, controller tune and score 0.1-0.2, 64 mutants x 16 lives plus re-score about 0.05, gap check about 0.02.

Shared across an arm's 12 seeds:
- 2 candidates per 25 generations adds about 5-10%;
- 4 per 10 generations adds about 40-60%.

So about 1.1-1.5x. A full POET, with a population per world and 4-8 active worlds, would cost 4-8x.
risks: Admission is only as good as the information controller. A weak one misses worlds. One too strong through non-local pooling admits worlds no local tissue can solve. Mitigations: latency per lattice hop and the gap cap.
Screens are noisy: gap estimates are noisy (as PAIRED found), and the mutant test has a winner's curse unless the replicate stage is kept.
The key space is bounded, so admissions plateau, as original POET's ANNECS did.
Diversity collapse onto one family of worlds; base skills forgotten unless 25% base lives are kept.
F is not comparable across generations once the world set moves, so fixed yardsticks are needed.
The 'playing dead' lesson: screen and yardstick lives must be statistically identical to selection lives.
options.beyond_hand_evidence: An ANNECS-like count: the number of archived worlds where a final best beats every hand body (frozen and re-tuned in that world, on separate tuning lives) by more than 3 SE on 1,024 fresh lives, with lateral_off, hidden_off or a genes_blind fork removing at least 50% of the lead. Above all, any such world from the families the old plan excluded (blink, lead, flip, decoy). Also transfer: archive-trained bests beat arm B's bests on the plan's held-out worlds H1-H7.

options.name: Broad domain randomisation over all task keys (the no-feedback control)
options.plain_explanation: Each life draws every task key at random from wide ranges that are fixed once, before the run. With the within-life bundle, keys can also switch inside a life on a random telegraph process. Nothing depends on the population. This is 'variety alone': the control that tells whether options 1 and 2 worked because of feedback or just because of variety. My proposal is to draw exactly option 1's prey-genome space uniformly. That makes it Zaman's 'no feedback' control at no extra design cost.
options.what_changes: WORLD and KERNEL: none for repo keys. Within-life switches use kernel_x (scratch) or the plan's epoch bundle (repo). OUTER LOOP: the plan's E3 family harness (hash-keyed per-life draw, stratified slots), configured with wide ranges instead of six members. Prices and d0 fixed.
options.locality: Per-life keys, plus within-life switches under plan 2.5's rules. Organism rules are unchanged, and no draw is visible to cells except through receptor pings.
options.user_decision: The ranges, which I recommend tying to option 1's prey space. Whether within-life switches may be included (Q4). Whether this runs as its own arm or only as the control for arms C and A.
options.engineering_pd: 2 pd with E3 for repo keys; plus 3.5-4 pd (and 1-1.5 pd for JS) for repo-grade within-life switches, or about 1 pd using kernel_x in scratch.
options.cpu: About 1.0-1.3x per life: bright and decoy draws generate more receptor candidates. Per-life spread in F rises, so matching today's selection information may need about 1.5x lives.
risks: The average world rewards a robust reflex. Kashtan, Noor & Alon 2007 found that scoring many goals at once gives virtually no speedup.
PAIRED found domain randomisation fails on hard transfer (0% where PAIRED reached 18-40%).
Many draws pay only the reflex, so 'be smaller' selection in hard draws.
Higher noise for the same CPU.
options.beyond_hand_evidence: The plan's held-out generalisation count (section 2.8) against each held-out world's best reflex, with lesions. I mainly expect robustness, not new capability. Its value is the comparison: if arm C or A beats arm D on held-out prey and worlds, feedback did the work.

options.name: Modularly varying goals (plan arm M), later with goal pairs drawn from the archive
options.plain_explanation: The whole population's world alternates between two goals every E generations on a fixed calendar that ignores the population (Kashtan & Alon). The goals share a subproblem and differ in one part. In the literature this built modular circuits and sped evolution. The current pair (pool and noisy) needs no new circuit, so it cannot reach capabilities beyond hand design on its own. The automatic version draws the pair from option 2's archive: two worlds whose rankings of the fixed body archive partly overlap (PATA-EC). A shared ranking is a capability-agnostic stand-in for 'shares a subproblem'. Keep the fixed-calendar pool/noisy arm as the clean control.
options.what_changes: No kernel change. The generation calendar (plan E4, 0.5 pd) and gate G4 (re-adaptation time sets E once). The automatic pairing needs option 2's archive and novelty code.
options.locality: The world is fixed within a generation and life. The calendar runs over generations and no cell can sense it.
options.user_decision: Already plan decision 3 (approve the fixed calendar). New question: once the archive exists, may the pair be chosen from it? That choice is population-dependent the same way option 2 is.
options.engineering_pd: 0.5 pd (E4), already in the plan. Automatic pairing: about 1 pd on top of option 2.
options.cpu: 1.0x per generation, plus gate G4 (about 40 generations of one population).
risks: The pool/noisy pair tests switching, not new capability.
E must sit in a working window; G4 sets it once and it never changes.
Shown only on small logic and feedforward networks, not on developmental GRN tissues.
The automatic pairing inherits option 2's risks.
options.beyond_hand_evidence: Re-adaptation time shrinks across switches, toward 5 generations or fewer. Generations to the first R1-level router compared with arms P and F. For archive pairs: final bests beat hand bodies, by more than 3 SE with lesions, in both goals of a pair where hand bodies fail in at least one.

options.name: Intraspecific competition: rivals from the population share one world
options.plain_explanation: Two bodies share one screen and race for the same target; the first click within the capture radius wins it. To keep comparisons fair, each life slot gets one rival drawn from the previous generation's elite or a hall of fame. Every candidate in a generation meets the same rivals on the same lives. As the population improves, so do its rivals: the population becomes its own environment. Optionally bodies glow faintly, so a body can notice a rival, but only through its own receptors. Following, shadowing and avoiding then become possible. This is the purest form of 'new individuals create new opportunities' (Soros & Stanley's condition 2), but it is the most expensive to build.
options.locality: Each body's cells run their usual local rules. The rival is just part of the world, seen only through the body's own receptors d_min later. Each body keeps its own clocks. The merged scheduler is the world's exact time order, not a clock either body can read.
options.user_decision: Whether to break today's one-body ABI, a large change across three engines. The arena geometry. Whether bodies glow (are visible to each other). Who the rivals are (elite, hall of fame, a mix). How a shared target is re-placed (around a random body, uniformly, or around the loser).
options.engineering_pd: Repo grade 12-20 pd: kernel 4-6, reference 3-4, JS 2-3, ABI and tests 2-3, pairing 1-2. Scratch kernel only: 6-9 pd.
options.cpu: About 2x per generation with a simulated rival in every life, since the rival's cells cost as much as the candidate's, keeping common random numbers. Random pairing costs about 1x CPU but loses common random numbers, so ranking then needs about 2x lives anyway.
risks: Heavy engineering before the first result, across three engines that must stay bit-identical.
Scramble competition rewards speed and clicking first, which a reflex already does well. It may select bigger or faster reflexes rather than computation.
Collusion or mediocre stable states, and cycling.
Bugs in new multi-body code that evolution then exploits (Sims).
Many new world design choices (arena, placement, visibility), each a possible hidden designer bias.
options.beyond_hand_evidence: The evolved best beats every hand body (re-tuned reflex, routers) when both face (a) the run's elite rivals, (b) hand-reflex rivals and (c) other seeds' rivals, and still beats them alone in base. Lesions remove at least 50% of the lead. Visible behaviours no hand body has, such as cutting off a rival's target or shadowing a rival.

options.name: Competitive income sharing across shared lives (Rosin & Belew)
options.plain_explanation: Each shared life is treated as a resource. A body's income on a life is divided by the population's mean income on that life. Costs are never shared. Lives that most bodies fail on become worth more, so bodies that catch what others miss are rewarded, without saying why. It is the cheapest way to make the population part of the environment, but it changes what selection means.
options.what_changes: Outer loop only: per-life normalisation of income in the scratch evolve loop. No kernel or world change.
options.locality: Pure outer loop; in-life rules and worlds are untouched.
options.user_decision: A departure from 'fitness = task performance': selection would use shared income minus costs, not plain F. Because costs are not shared, the exchange rate between income and cell cost would move with the population. When the population does well on a life, its income is devalued relative to costs, which quietly changes the size bound. That conflicts with 'growth bounded by physics plus costs', so I do not recommend it except as a short diagnostic arm.
risks: It changes the price of a cell depending on the population, which can push toward shrinking.
With only 3 + 4 lives per generation, most per-life difficulty is Poisson noise, so the reward amplifies noise.
It breeds brittle niche specialists unless the population is read as a set.
Raw F must still be reported, and it can diverge from the selected score.
options.beyond_hand_evidence: Niche count: distinct final strategies, each beating the best reflex in some held-out worlds, against arm B's count. A body beating hand bodies on plain F would still be required.
